question: What assessment and monitoring steps should an agency plan from designing a new in-scope AI use case through deployment and later material changes?
draft:
**Design phase (before deployment)**

Agencies must assess all new AI use cases against the in-scope criteria (Appendix C) to determine whether they fall within the policy; the assessment must be documented and take place during the design phase while developing requirements [2]. For use cases determined to be in-scope, agencies must conduct an AI use case impact assessment, commencing it at the design stage, and must finalise the assessment and apply any agreed risk treatments before the solution is deployed [2].

Agencies may conduct the impact assessment using either the Australian Government AI impact assessment tool or an internal process that integrates all provisions of the tool [1]. Where an agency integrates the tool, it must ensure the internal process is consistent and delivers the same (or a higher) risk outcome for inherent and residual risk, and must be able to revise its internal process in response to any impact assessment tool updates [1].

**Registration and deployment-stage monitoring**

Agencies must add each in-scope AI use case to their internal register of AI use cases and update it as required, including risk rating and accountable use case owner changes [1]. When deploying an in-scope AI use case, agencies must regularly monitor and evaluate the use case to ensure it is operating as intended and that risks are being effectively managed, and must re-validate the AI use case impact assessment by checking its accuracy and updating it when there is a material change in the use case scope, usage or operation [1].

Agencies should also monitor changes not initiated by the agency — for example, vendor changes and changes in the regulatory environment — and could ask vendors to provide information on updates through contractual mechanisms [1].

**Risk-tiered governance**

Where an in-scope use case has an inherent medium-risk rating, agencies should consider whether it would benefit from being governed through a designated board or a senior executive, choosing an approach appropriate to the size and scope of the agency if additional governance is applied [3]. Where the inherent rating is high-risk, agencies must report the use case to the agency accountable official with the reasons for the rating, proposed mitigations and residual risks, and must govern it through a designated board or a senior executive, whichever is appropriate to the agency's size and scope [3]. Once the agency has decided to deploy, it must report the use case to the DTA through the accountable official and establish a system to regularly review the use case at least every 12 months, with the review reporting to the relevant governing board or senior executive on whether the use case is operating as intended and risks are being effectively managed, and considering the impact assessment and any revisions to it [3].

**Out-of-scope use cases and material change**

For use cases assessed as out of scope, agencies may adopt the use case while ensuring compliance with relevant existing obligations such as privacy and security; if adopted, they must assess whether the use case becomes in-scope if there is a material change in the scope, usage or operation of the solution [4]. If a use case is in scope, agencies must follow any applicable actions in the policy [4].

**Timing**

Agencies must begin AI use case assessments within 12 months of the policy taking effect, and for existing use cases not yet assessed must determine whether they are in scope and apply all relevant policy actions by 30 April 2027; where practicable, agencies should implement requirements ahead of these deadlines [2]. Agencies should implement requirements sooner if practicable and could consider interim processes while building out their approach toward the specified implementation deadline [7].

**Evidence gaps**

The provided excerpts do not establish specific monitoring cadence or re-validation triggers for medium-risk use cases beyond the general deployment-stage monitoring and re-validation duties, nor do they specify the content or format of the internal register beyond risk rating and accountable use case owner changes.

Mandatory requirements

All new AI use cases Agencies must assess all new AI use cases against the in-scope criteria (Appendix C) to determine if they are in scope of the policy. Where practicable, agencies should implement the requirements ahead of the deadlines listed above.

child_citations.title: Policy for the Responsible Use of AI in Government
child_citations.quote:
This policy has been designed to exclude incidental and lower risk uses of AI that do not meet the criteria.

Incidental uses of AI may include off-the-shelf software with AI features such as grammar checks and internet searches with AI functionality. The policy recognises that incidental usage of AI will grow over time and focuses on uses that require additional oversight and governance. 1 As defined by the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).

2 As defined by the Australian Government Protective Security Policy Framework

In assessing whether a use case is in scope, agencies should also carefully consider AI use in the following areas: • recruitment and other employment-related decision making • automated decision making of discretionary decisions • administration of justice and democratic processes • law enforcement, profiling individuals, and border control • health • education • critical infrastructure. While use cases in these areas are not automatically high-risk, they are more likely to involve risks that require careful attention through an impact assessment.

Experimentation For the avoidance of doubt, agencies are not required to apply this policy if they are doing early-stage experimentation which does not: • commit to proceeding with a use case or to any design decisions that would affect implementation later • risk harming anyone • introduce or exacerbate any privacy or security risks. If there is a likelihood of proceeding with the AI use case while experimenting in this phase, agencies should apply the policy. Agencies should also apply the Australian Government AI technical standard, which provides relevant information for developing use cases at each stage of the AI lifecycle.

AI use cases in scope of this policy (referred to as in-scope AI use cases) are use cases that meet any criteria in Appendix C. child_citations.section_title: 2.2.1 Clear allocation of responsibilities within and outside the organisation
child_citations.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
child_citations.quote:
The system uses three coordinated agents in a primarily sequential workflow, with feedback loops for additional retrieval or restructuring where needed:

The responsibilities below describe how operating accountability for this report -drafting use case is allocated, within the context of PwC Singapore’s broader AI governance framework:

1. Use case owner – Use case appropriateness and accountable use: Confirming that the use case serves a legitimate business need, is appropriate for the intended purpose, and is aligned with the organisation’s AI governance framework. The use case owner remains accountable for the responsible use of the application and for ensuring that appropriate human oversight is in place.

2. Technology Risk Management Team – Risk assessment and control advice: Supports the assessment of technology, risk, security, and compliance considerations for the use case, including any regulatory requirements . This includes advising on appropriate controls relating to tools and models, access rights, and connected knowledge bases or data sources.

3. AI Factory – Design, development, guardrails and monitoring: Designing, developing, and maintaining the application, including prompt design, model selection, tool configuration, integration with approved knowledge bases , and appropriate guardrails . AI Factory also monitors for model changes and manages updates through standard change management processes rather than leaving it to the end users.
